I am thinking, for no particular reason, about a kitchen at three in the morning.

Not a dramatic kitchen. Not the scene of a revelation or a disaster. Just a small room with a refrigerator humming a little too loudly, a chipped blue mug on the counter, and that particular quality of light that comes from a streetlamp outside the window mixing with the pale glow above the stove. At three in the morning, ordinary objects stop performing their daytime roles. The chairs are not for sitting. The table is not for eating. They are just shapes that have agreed, temporarily, to be still. And the person standing there in socks, opening the refrigerator and forgetting why, is not really looking for food. They are looking for a reason to be awake in a world that is mostly asleep, and for proof that the house will remember how to be a house again when morning comes.

I think we spend most of our lives in that three-a.m. kitchen, metaphorically speaking. We stand between one completed thing and the next not-yet-begun thing, holding a glass of water, listening to the building settle. The grand narratives we tell ourselves — career, love, ambition, legacy — they work fine in daylight. At night they loosen. What remains are smaller truths: I am thirsty. I am a little lonely. The floor is cold. Tomorrow I should call my sister. I never learned how to fold a fitted sheet properly and probably never will. These are not lesser truths. They might be the only ones that never lie to us.

My grandmother kept buttons in a biscuit tin.

It was a round tin, once red, with a picture of a Scottish landscape faded to a kind of optimistic grey. Inside were hundreds of buttons that belonged to no living garment: pearl buttons, wooden toggles, brass uniform buttons, tiny shirt buttons so white they seemed to glow, one enormous Bakelite button that must have come from a coat worn by a giant in a story. Whenever a button fell off anything in her house, it went into the tin, not with any real expectation of reunion, but with the faith that separation should not mean disappearance. As a child I would pour them onto the carpet and sort them by color, then by size, then by imagined importance. The tin smelled faintly of metal and shortbread and old houses.

She is gone now, and I do not know where the tin went. Someone probably threw it away during the necessary cruelty of clearing a home. That is what we do. We stand in rooms full of a life and we ask, ruthlessly, what is useful, what is valuable, what can be kept in a smaller flat, what will anyone actually want. And a tin of orphaned buttons fails every test except the only one that mattered to her, which was: did someone once need this, and might they again?

I think about that tin more often than I think about many supposedly important things. I think we all have a version of it, even if ours is a drawer full of cables for phones we no longer own, or a phone full of photographs we never look at, or a mind full of faces from a school corridor thirty years ago whose names arrive in the shower without warning. We are collectors of loose buttons. We cannot help it. Letting go completely would feel less like tidying and more like erasure. So we keep. We keep ticket stubs and recipes written in handwriting that slopes uphill, voicemails we cannot delete because the voice in them no longer exists anywhere else. We keep because memory is an unreliable tenant and objects are its rent receipts.

Not far from where I imagine that kitchen, there is a sea. There is always a sea somewhere in my thinking, even when I am inland, even when the nearest coast is hours away. The sea is the original three-a.m. kitchen: restless, repetitive, indifferent, and strangely comforting because of its indifference. It does not need you to understand it. It was doing this before you arrived and it will continue after you have gone home with sand in your shoes.

I love the hour when people leave the beach. Early evening, the lifeguards packing up, families shaking out towels, children protesting with the full force of their lungs as if being taken away from the water were a historical injustice. Then quiet. The sea gets its room back. The waves seem louder not because they have changed but because we have stopped competing with them. I have stood on shorelines in that hour and felt the specific relief of being unimportant in a beautiful place. The universe is not sending me a message. The tide is not a metaphor unless I need it to be. It is just water obeying the moon, which is miracle enough without my decorating it.

And yet we decorate. We must. A fisherman sees weather. A child sees a monster’s bathtub. A poet sees grief with better rhythm. A geologist sees time turned liquid. All of them are right, which is another way of saying the sea is large enough to contain our projections without being reduced by them. I wish more things in life were like that. I wish opinions and memories and other people could receive what we pour into them and remain themselves. Perhaps they do, and we are only too impatient to notice.

If the sea is where I go to feel small in a good way, the library is where I go to feel less alone in my smallness.

A good library has a smell that no architect can design and no cleaning product can erase: paper, dust warmed by radiators, wooden shelves, the faint sweetness of old glue. It is the smell of many minds having been somewhere before you. I love the democratic chaos of it. In one aisle, a teenager is cramming for an exam she is convinced will decide her entire future. Two shelves over, a retired man is reading a biography of a general he despises, very slowly, with a pencil. Somewhere a toddler is treating a picture book as both literature and percussion instrument. Nobody is asked to justify their presence. You do not need a ticket, a membership to the right club, or a convincing explanation. You need, mostly, curiosity, or at least the desire for a warm chair and other people being quiet nearby.

Books have often been described as conversations with the dead, which is true but incomplete. They are also arguments with the living who are not in the room, rehearsals for lives we will never lead, and instructions left by strangers who assumed, generously, that we might show up one day needing to know how to fix a bicycle, identify a mushroom, or survive heartbreak in nineteenth-century Russia. Every library card is a small act of optimism: I believe I will return. I believe returning is possible. I believe the future version of me will still want to know things.

I sometimes imagine all the marginalia ever written — the underlinings, the exclamation marks, the furious little “no!” in a margin from 1974 — rising off the pages at night after closing, and having a meeting. What a parliament that would be. The romantics would sigh too loudly. The scientists would demand evidence. Some anonymous reader from Ohio who wrote “this happened to me” beside a paragraph and nothing else would bring the whole room to silence, because that is the entire history of reading in four words: this happened to me.

Between the sea and the library there is, inevitably, a walk through a city.

I am a devoted, inefficient walker. I take wrong turns with confidence. I stop to read plaques about people I have never heard of who did something admirable with water pressure in 1892. I look up at windows and invent the lives behind them with no evidence whatsoever: there, a violin teacher who is beloved and slightly feared; there, a couple who have just agreed, after a long discussion, to get a cat; there, a man eating toast alone and enjoying the solitude he pretends to complain about. Cities reward this kind of attention. They are collages pretending to be plans. A medieval lane leans against a glass tower; a bakery exhales into a bus stop; somebody has planted geraniums in a window box above a shop selling nothing you can identify, and the geraniums are thriving out of pure municipal stubbornness.

Walking also restores a proper relationship with time. In a car, distance is an inconvenience measured in minutes of delay. On a screen, the whole world is allegedly instant and therefore oddly weightless. On foot, a mile is a mile. It takes the time it takes, and during that time your thoughts are allowed to finish their sentences. Some of my best ideas have arrived at walking pace, not because walking is magic but because it bores the mind in the right way. The anxious, performative part of the brain gives up trying to be impressive and wanders off, and underneath it, quieter thoughts come out like animals at dusk. A solution to a letter I have been avoiding. The realization that I was wrong in an argument three weeks ago, in a specific way I can now name. The first line of something worth writing, which will, of course, have vanished by the time I find a pen, because the mind enjoys small cruelties.

If I walk long enough and in the right direction, I would like there to be a garden.

I am not a skilled gardener. My talents run toward hopeful planting and apologetic watering. But I love gardens precisely because they refuse to be hurried and refuse, also, to be fully controlled, which makes them honest teachers. You can prepare soil, you can read the packet, you can watch the forecast like a stockbroker, and still the slugs will hold their banquet and the one plant you neglected will produce an embarrassing abundance of flowers out of spite or joy. A garden is a collaboration with forces that have no interest in your self-esteem. Rain does not care that you had plans. Frost has not read your schedule. This is, after initial irritation, a relief.

There is a humility forced on anyone who has ever tried to grow tomatoes. The plant does not want your anxiety. It wants light, water, support, and to be left mostly alone to do the ancient work of turning sunlight into something red and improbable. People are not tomatoes — we require considerably more conversation and are worse at photosynthesizing compliments — but the lesson leaks across species. So many living things do not need us to hover. They need conditions, patience, and occasional intervention. Love, I suspect, is often gardening mistaken for architecture. We think we are building each other. More often we are just trying not to block the light.

Seeds, too, are an outrageous gamble that we perform casually. We put a dry, dead-looking speck into dirt and then act as though a green shoot is a reasonable expectation. It is not reasonable. It is a resurrection staged at windowsill scale, and we respond by saying, “Oh good, the basil’s up.” Humans are at their best, I think, when wonder becomes routine without becoming dull. The first time a child sees a sprout, they gasp correctly. The adult says, “Water it on Thursdays,” and in that sentence is the whole tragedy and triumph of growing up: we learn how to keep miracles alive by putting them in the calendar.

Somewhere between the garden and the library, language is growing wild.

I collect lost and endangered words the way my grandmother collected buttons. Did you know there is an old word, “apricity,” for the warmth of the sun in winter? That specific, stolen sweetness on your face in January while your hands are still cold in your pockets — someone treasured it enough to name it. There is “psithurism,” the sound of wind in trees. There is the Scots word “tartle,” for that panicked hesitation when you are about to introduce someone whose name you have forgotten. Everyone has tartled. Everyone has stood there with a smile bolted on, saying, “And this is...” while their brain ransacked burning archives. A language that has a word for that embarrassment is a language paying attention to real life.

Words disappear when the experiences they name become rare, or when we become too embarrassed to admit we still have the experiences. We lose words for kinds of snow when winters soften. We lose words for tools when the trades that used them fade. We gain others, of course — every generation coins bright slang that will embarrass it in photographs later — but each lost word is a small window painted shut. The feeling may still exist, wandering the house, but it has one fewer door to enter by.

That is why I write things down, I suppose. Not because my observations are uniquely valuable, but because notation is a form of hospitality. A sentence says: this moment was here, it can sit down. The bus driver who sang quietly to the radio at dawn. The way my friend laughs before she knows why she is laughing, as if her body got the joke first. The old man in the park feeding pigeons with the seriousness of a diplomat distributing aid. If no one writes them, do they vanish? Not entirely. The world is not so fragile. But our shared memory of the world becomes thinner, more reliant on headlines, and headlines were never designed to carry the weight of ordinary tenderness.

Ordinary tenderness is most visible, to me, among strangers.

I love trains for this reason. A train is a temporary village moving at speed, full of people who have agreed by unspoken treaty to be near each other without demanding anything. They share armrests and sighs and the announcement that the buffet car has, once again, a limited service. They witness each other’s small surrenders: the businessman asleep with his mouth open, suddenly eight years old; the student mouthing vocabulary; the woman knitting something that may become a sweater or may become a long, woolen intention. When the train stops unexpectedly between stations, a brief society forms. People make eye contact. Someone jokes. Someone shares a mint as if mints were now the local currency. Then we move again, and the society dissolves without sadness, having completed itself.

We are told, constantly, to fear strangers, and of course there are reasons, and of course caution is a form of intelligence. But a life organized entirely around suspicion becomes a very small room. Most strangers are not threats or angels; they are protagonists of stories we will never hear, carrying shopping and worries and a song stuck in their heads. The woman across the aisle is not “a passenger.” She is someone who once, at sixteen, cut her own hair and regretted it within the hour, who knows exactly how her mother takes tea, who may be traveling toward the hardest conversation of her year while highlighting a magazine article about houseplants. To imagine that, briefly and without intrusion, is not sentimentality. It is accuracy. Everyone is more specific than the role they occupy in our day.

At night, when the trains have stopped and the garden is dark and the library is locked, there are stars, performing their old trick of making time visible.

Astronomy is the rudest and kindest science. It tells you that you are made of materials forged in ancient stellar violence, which means that “star stuff” is not a pretty line but a materials report. And then, having dismantled your importance with one hand, it gives you the night sky for free, every clear night, no ticket required, the original public library of light. Kind and rude. I find it helps to be regularly outscaled. My embarrassment at something I said in 2016 has survived years of feeding; under Orion it looks, correctly, like a very small animal I have been keeping as a pet. I can let it go. The universe is under no obligation to make us feel significant, and I have come to prefer it that way. Meaning that is handed to us cheaply tends to expire quickly. If I could send a letter to the future, it would not contain predictions. Predictions are just the present wearing a false moustache. I would send a list of things I hope still exist, and a confession of things I hope we have outgrown.

I hope there are still libraries where a person can be warm and unproductive in public without shame. I hope someone is still keeping a tin of useless, beautiful salvage. I hope children are taught the names of trees with the same seriousness as the names of brands, and that some adult, somewhere, still says “apricity” out loud on a cold bright morning and makes another person repeat it, delighted. I hope we still walk places slowly enough to invent the lives behind windows, and that we hold those inventions lightly, knowing the real lives are better. I hope strangers on stalled trains still share mints. I hope we have become braver about tenderness and more suspicious of cruelty dressed as realism. I hope we have learned that attention is not a passive act but a moral one: what we notice, we protect; what we ignore, we allow to be taken.

And I hope, in that future, someone stands in a kitchen at three in the morning, in socks, holding a glass of water for no clear reason, and feels — not happy, exactly, not solved — but accompanied. By the hum of the refrigerator. By the long human history of being awake when the world is quiet. By all the small salvaged moments rattling gently in the tin.

Morning will come, as it rudely and mercifully does. The chairs will become chairs again. The buttons will go back to being junk to anyone who did not know their owner. The tide will not explain itself, the basil will want watering, a word will be on the tip of the tongue, a train will fill with villages, and the stars will hand their shift over to the sun without ceremony. Nothing will be finished. Everything will be continuing. And we will get up, and make tea badly or well, and take our place again in the unfinished, unglamorous, unbearably precious middle of things — which is, and has always been, the only place life actually happens.

By the hum of the refrigerator. By the long human history of being awake when the world is quiet. By all the small salvaged moments rattling gently in the tin.

Morning will come, as it rudely and mercifully does. The chairs will become chairs again. The buttons will go back to being junk to anyone who did not know their owner. The tide will not explain itself, the basil will want watering, a word will be on the tip of the tongue, a train will fill with villages, and the stars will hand their shift over to the sun without ceremony. Nothing will be finished. Everything will be continuing. And we will get up, and make tea badly or well, and take our place again in the unfinished, unglamorous, unbearably precious middle of things — which is, and has always been, the only place life actually happens.
